_note: The model never types an author, a title or a year. It returns an id and a claim index, and code substitutes the strings below. That makes a fabricated citation structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely, which matters because a made-up study on a psychology page is the one mistake there is no recovering from. Claims are pre-written for the same reason: a real source can still be misrepresented. Every line here must pass source_is_specific() in audit_copy.py, which the test suite asserts.

citations.line: — Russell Barkley, *Taking Charge of Adult ADHD* (2010)
claims: Barkley found that a fuzzy sense of time parks people in standby, so the hours before something fixed get held rather than used.
Barkley describes starting as a separate skill from wanting to start, which is why intention alone does not move you.

citations.line: — Edward Hallowell and John Ratey, *Driven to Distraction* (1994)
claims: Hallowell describes a mind holding every option open at once, which leaves you hovering rather than choosing one.
Hallowell found that interest, not importance, is what switches attention on, so the urgent task is often the one you cannot reach.
Cowan measured working memory at about four items at once. Seventeen open loops do not fit, so the task itself falls out.
Cowan showed that holding more than a handful of things in mind pushes the earliest one out without you noticing it go.

citations.line: — Sophie Leroy, *Why Is It So Hard to Do My Work?* (2009)
claims: Leroy showed attention leaves a residue on every unfinished thing, so each open task keeps taking a small cut of your focus.
Leroy found that switching tasks before finishing leaves part of your attention behind on the one you left.
Walker describes brief wakings between sleep cycles as ordinary. What breaks a night is the alarm you sound about them.
Walker found that evening light and alertness push the sleep signal later, so the body waits for a gap that never opens.

citations.line: — Colin Espie, *Overcoming Insomnia and Sleep Problems* (2006)
claims: Espie found that checking the time turns a normal waking into a maths problem, and the maths finishes waking you up.
Espie showed that trying harder to sleep makes sleep less likely, because effort is the opposite of what the state requires.
LeDoux showed the alarm circuit fires before you have read a single word, so the body is already braced by the time you look.
LeDoux found the brain runs threat rehearsals to prepare you, which is useful for predators and useless for a short email.

citations.line: — Susan Nolen-Hoeksema, *Women Who Think Too Much* (2003)
claims: Nolen-Hoeksema found rehearsal feels like problem solving while producing no new information, so the loop keeps running.
Nolen-Hoeksema showed that going over a moment again lowers mood rather than resolving it, which then makes going over it easier.
Brewer showed a loop repeats when it reliably lowers discomfort, so the habit gets stronger every night it works.
Brewer found that naming what a habit actually gives you is what loosens it, more than deciding to stop.
The Nagoskis showed a stress cycle needs a clear ending signal. Without one the body stays braced long after the work stopped.
The Nagoskis found that removing the stressor is not the same as completing the stress, and the body only responds to the second.
Maslach found that when worth is measured in output, stopping feels like losing standing rather than finishing the day.
Maslach showed burnout builds from a mismatch between a person and their workload, not from a weakness in the person.

citations.line: — Nedra Glover Tawwab, *Set Boundaries, Find Peace* (2021)
claims: Tawwab found that over explaining invites negotiation, because every reason you list becomes something to argue with.
Tawwab describes a boundary as information about you rather than a demand on someone else, which is why it needs no case.
Lerner describes learning that refusal is only safe when justified, which turns a short answer into a case.
Lerner showed that changing your part in a pattern reliably provokes a push to put it back, and that the push is not proof you were wrong.

citations.line: — Pete Walker, *Complex PTSD: From Surviving to Thriving* (2013)
claims: Walker describes a survival style built on smoothing things first, which turns an apology into the entry fee for taking up space.
Walker found that appeasing is learned where it worked, which is why it arrives before you have decided anything.
Neff found that treating yourself as you would a friend improves follow through, while self criticism predicts giving up.
Neff showed that recognising a difficulty as ordinary and shared does more for recovery than judging yourself for having it.
Clear describes each action as a vote for an identity, which means two sentences still counts as a vote for the person who writes.
Clear found that making the first move smaller beats making the goal bigger, because starting is the part that fails.
Gollwitzer found that naming when and where you will act roughly doubles follow through compared with deciding to try.
Gollwitzer showed that an if then plan hands the decision to the situation, so you do not have to make it while under pressure.
Porges showed that people raised around unpredictable moods keep a background scanner running, so neutral tone reads as warning.
Porges found the body decides whether a situation is safe before you have consciously assessed it.
